subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Default Organ Donation
description: A quick win: understand Default Organ Donation.

hook.text: Austria has 99% organ donor consent. Germany has 12%. The countries are neighbors.

buildup.text: Default effects in organ donation save thousands of lives. When the default is yes, almost nobody opts out.

discovery.text: Johnson and Goldstein proved the effect is about effort, not preference. Most people support donation but never fill.

twist.text: Mandated choice is a middle path. Everyone must choose yes or no when renewing a license.

climax.text: Organ donation defaults demonstrate the single most powerful lesson: the option people get without acting shapes.

punchline.text: The default saves more lives than any campaign ever could.

quiz.question: Why does Austria have 99% organ donor consent compared to Germany's 12%?
options: Austrians are more altruistic than Germans
Austria uses opt-out while Germany uses opt-in defaults
Austria pays organ donors but Germany does not

details.summary: Default organ donation policies switch from opt-in to opt-out, meaning citizens are presumed donors unless they actively refuse. Countries with opt-out defaults have organ donation consent rates above 90 percent compared to below 20 percent for opt-in countries.
details.whyItMatters: The organ donation default is the most dramatic example of how defaults shape life-and-death outcomes. The difference between opt-in and opt-out saves thousands of lives annually by aligning inertia with the socially beneficial outcome.
takeaways: Opt-out countries achieve over 90 percent donation consent rates
Opt-in countries struggle to reach 20 percent consent rates
The default effect is amplified by the emotional difficulty of the topic

faq.question: Why does the opt-in versus opt-out default matter so much?
faq.answer: Organ donation is emotionally difficult to think about. Most people avoid the decision entirely. Under opt-in, avoidance means no donation. Under opt-out, avoidance means donation. The default captures the behavior of the undecided majority.

faq.question: Do opt-out countries actually transplant more organs?
faq.answer: Not always proportionally to consent rates. Actual transplantation depends on infrastructure, family overrides, and medical factors. But opt-out countries still transplant significantly more organs because the larger consent pool provides more eligible donors.
